The Knout goby (Mesogobius batrachocephalus) is a large-bodied gobiid inhabiting the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, where it occupies coastal rocky and sandy habitats. Field surveys indicate that maximum body size in this species approaches a total length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters], which is considerably larger than most other gobiids in the region such as the common gudgeon (Gobio gobio). The relationship between length and mass in this species, derived from extensive sampling, reveals that an individual attaining this ultimate length reaches approximately 371 grams [Wwi = approximately 371 grams] in wet weight. At a stable water temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active females averaged 21% [GSI = 21%].

Female Knout gobies reach sexual maturity at a notably smaller body size compared to their ultimate dimensions, with puberty commencing at a total length of 18 centimeters [Lp = 18 centimeters]. Using the length-weight relationship established for this species, the corresponding wet weight at this pubertal length is calculated to be 52.6 grams [Wwp = 52.6 grams]. This threshold is considerably lower than the maximum adult mass, suggesting that individuals begin allocating resources toward reproduction well before completing somatic growth. Compared to the similar-sized Gobio gobio, for which females mature at approximately 13 centimeters relative to an ultimate length of 21 centimeters, the Knout goby exhibits a comparable proportional delay in maturation relative to its maximum size. Sexual maturation in this species is accompanied by pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males typically developing a broader head and more robust pectoral fins during the breeding season.

The early life stages of Mesogobius batrachocephalus reflect a reproductive strategy characterized by the production of relatively large, nutrient-rich eggs. Based on an average egg diameter of 2.7 millimeters, the calculated wet weight at birth for a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is approximately 0.01 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.01 grams]. This substantial initial mass provides the lecithotrophic larva with sufficient endogenous yolk reserves to sustain it through the critical period of mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. At the typical thermal regime of 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the incubation period for the fertilised eggs lasts approximately two to three weeks before eclosion occurs. The hatching event releases a prolarva that is already well-developed, with pigmented eyes and a functional circulatory system visible through its transparent body. These yolk-sac larvae remain largely sedentary, adhering to substrates near the nest site until the yolk is fully resorbed and the trophic switch to active feeding begins.

Longevity records for the Knout goby indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days] at a water temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly eight years, is relatively uncommon among gobiid fishes of comparable body size, many of which complete their life cycles in three to four years. The species exhibits an iteroparous reproductive strategy, spawning multiple times over successive breeding seasons, which likely contributes to its sustained population densities in stable coastal environments. The natural mortality rate appears to be highest during the first year of life, particularly during the pelagic larval phase and the post-settlement juvenile stage when predation pressure from piscivorous fishes is most intense. Adult survivorship is comparatively high, supported by the species' cryptic benthic lifestyle and well-developed nest-guarding behavior, where males aggressively defend egg clutches deposited under rocks or within crevices.

Spawning activity in the Knout goby typically occurs during the spring months when water temperatures begin to rise above 10 °C. Reproductively active females, recognized by their distended abdomens and visible urogenital papilla, deposit adhesive eggs onto the undersides of stones or into excavated cavities. The gonadosomatic index of reproductively active females reached 21% [GSI = 21%] at 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. The male remains with the clutch throughout the incubation period, fanning the eggs to maintain oxygenation and aggressively warding off potential egg predators. After the larvae hatch and become free-swimming, they enter a brief planktonic phase before settling into benthic habitats as post-metamorphic juveniles. This combination of large egg size, paternal care, and a relatively long lifespan characterizes the Knout goby as a K-selected strategist within its gobiid community.
